candidates.claim: The flat genes are flat because their products are not biomass precursors - the objective never demands what they make, so deleting them is free by construction. This explains the 71% of flat genes that isozyme GPR structure does not.

The failure is not a defect to fix but a SCREEN to use: a gene FBA keeps flat everywhere while the data calls it conditionally essential is, by construction, a gene whose condition-dependence comes from REGULATION rather than stoichiometry. The 110 flat genes are therefore a label-free PREDICTION of regulatory control, testable against known regulons.

Crossing the gap-fill dead-end with the pFBA dead-end inverts both: gap-fill showed ADDING reactions worsens flatness and pFBA showed removing them indiscriminately worsens accuracy, so the model is too LARGE - a smaller curated core E. coli model should predict conditional essentiality better than iML1515 despite covering less biochemistry.

Relax the assumption that RB-TnSeq competitive fitness and FBA monoculture growth measure the same thing: a gene can be competitively unfit in a pool while remaining monoculture-viable, so the flatness is a label-modality mismatch rather than a model defect.

The unit of prediction is wrong. FBA is a reaction-flux model and gene-level deletion is a lossy projection through the GPR; scoring conditional essentiality at the REACTION level rather than the gene level would remove the isozyme-masking that makes 29% of flat genes flat by construction.

Relax the single-objective assumption: iML1515 maximises one biomass reaction, but a cell on a poor carbon source is not maximising growth. Replacing the objective with a condition-appropriate one (e.g. ATP yield, or a measured growth-rate constraint) would restore the condition-specificity that flat ratios lack.
